pos: n. (firstborn son of Judah by the daughter of Shua; Hebrew Er)
etymology: Hebrew Er, commonly derived from a root meaning to watch or be awake. The name of a watchman was given to a man whose wickedness the LORD watched and answered.
biblical_def: Er is the firstborn of Judah by the daughter of Shua the Canaanitess, and the whole of his recorded life is three facts: he was born, he was given Tamar to wife, and “Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD; and the LORD slew him” (Gen 38:7). Scripture does not name the wickedness. It names the sight in which it was wickedness and the hand that answered it. The Chronicler, compiling the royal genealogy centuries later, repeats the verdict rather than quietly dropping it: Er was evil in the sight of the LORD, and he slew him (1Ch 2:3). This is the more striking because the line is the Messianic line. The chapter that records Er's death goes on to Onan's death, to Judah's sin with Tamar at Enaim, and to the birth of Pharez — and Pharez stands in the genealogy of our Lord. Er is the eldest son of the royal tribe, the natural head of the line of promise, and he is removed from it by God directly. The birthright ran on without him.

webster_full: The proper name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary.
ER. The firstborn son of Judah by the daughter of Shua, a Canaanitess.
The Hebrew is commonly referred to a root signifying to watch, or to be awake.
He was married to Tamar, and died childless under the judgment of God.
A second Er appears in the genealogy of our Lord in Luke 3:28.
scriptures: Gen 38:3
And she conceived, and bare a son; and he called his name Er.
Gen 38:6
And Judah took a wife for Er his firstborn, whose name was Tamar.
Gen 38:7
And Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD; and the LORD slew him.

The sons of Judah; Er, and Onan, and Shelah: which three were born unto him of the daughter of Shua the Canaanitess. And Er, the firstborn of Judah, was evil in the sight of the LORD; and he slew him.
corruption_summary: The silence about Er's particular sin is treated as a gap to be filled, when the text is deliberately withholding the detail and reporting only the verdict.
corruption_paragraphs: Because Genesis says what God thought of Er without saying what Er did, commentators and story-tellers have supplied the missing offence, and readers come away arguing about a speculation. The text's reticence is not an oversight. Onan's sin, by contrast, is described exactly, because the point there is the refusal of the levirate duty; Er's is withheld, because the point here is the verdict itself. He was wicked in the sight of the LORD — that phrase locates the standard outside the man, outside his family, and outside the customs of the Canaanite house Judah had married into. What the neighbours thought is not recorded either.

The principle to recover is that birth into the line of promise saves nobody. Er stood in the most privileged position available to a man in his generation: eldest son of Judah, heir of the tribe from which Shiloh would come. It did not shelter him for an hour. And the chapter that removes him does not thereby break the promise — it goes on through Tamar and Pharez to David and to Christ, by a route no one would have chosen. God is not dependent on the firstborn, the obvious heir, or the respectable branch. He kept His word through the family He had just judged.

pos: n. (father of Elishama, prince of Ephraim; Hebrew Ammihud)
etymology: Hebrew Ammihud, ‘my people is majesty’ or ‘people of splendour’ — a name compounded of am, people, and hod, majesty.
biblical_def: Ammihud appears in Scripture almost entirely as somebody's father. He is named four times in Numbers, and every time it is as the son of Ammihud attached to Elishama, captain of the children of Ephraim — in the muster at Sinai, in the order of the western camp, at the head of Ephraim's armies, and on the seventh day of the offerings at the dedication of the altar. Ammihud himself does nothing in the narrative. He is a patronymic, a hinge on which a more prominent man is identified. Yet the Chronicler, tracing Ephraim's line, sets him in a chain that runs Laadan, Ammihud, Elishama (1Ch 7:26) — and that chain runs on to Nun, and from Nun to Joshua. The man who is only ever a father in Numbers is great-grandfather to the captain who brought Israel over Jordan. Other men bear the name: the father of Shemuel of Simeon, of Pedahel of Naphtali, and the father of Talmai king of Geshur, whose daughter bore Absalom.

webster_full: The proper name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary.
AMMIHUD. The father of Elishama, prince of the tribe of Ephraim in the wilderness.
The name is compounded of am, people, and hod, majesty or splendour.
Through Elishama and Nun his line descends to Joshua the son of Nun.
The name is borne also by men of Simeon, of Naphtali, and by the father of the king of Geshur.
scriptures: Num 1:10
Of the children of Joseph: of Ephraim; Elishama the son of Ammihud: of Manasseh; Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur.
Num 2:18
On the west side shall be the standard of the camp of Ephraim according to their armies: and the captain of the sons of Ephraim shall be Elishama the son of Ammihud.
Num 7:48
On the seventh day Elishama the son of Ammihud, prince of the children of Ephraim, offered:
Laadan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son,
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a man may serve his generation chiefly by whom he raises.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Ammihud is far too obscure a name to be contested; the risk is only that a reader passes over the patronymics as noise between the numbers.

The principle to recover is the honour God puts on fatherhood as such. Ammihud has no recorded deed, no speech, and no death notice. He is named four times solely to identify his son, and a fifth time to be a link between his own father and that son. By every measure the world uses he is invisible, and yet the line he stands in produces Joshua. Scripture is full of this pattern — the promise runs through households, and the LORD who commanded Israel to teach these words diligently unto their children was building His nation four generations at a time. Many a Christian man's life work will read like Ammihud's in the record: a name, a son, and a line that goes somewhere he did not live to see.

“On the seventh day” — his son's turn among the twelve princes.

pos: n. (prince of Dan in the wilderness; also chief of the Benjamite archers who came to David at Ziklag; Hebrew Achiezer)
etymology: Hebrew Achiezer, ‘my brother is help’ — from ach, brother, and ezer, help, the same word used of the help God is to His people.
biblical_def: Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai is prince of the tribe of Dan through the wilderness years. He is numbered at Sinai, set as captain over the standard of the camp of Dan on the north side, and brings his offering on the tenth day at the dedication of the altar. Dan marched last, in the rearward of all the camps, gathering up the stragglers — and Ahiezer led that rear guard for forty years. A second man of the name appears at one of the darkest moments of David's life: while David was yet kept close because of Saul, armed men came to him at Ziklag, and “the chief was Ahiezer” (1Ch 12:3), of Saul's own tribe of Benjamin, able to use both the right hand and the left in slinging stones and shooting arrows. Both men bear a name that is a confession — my brother is help — and both are found where help was actually needed: at the back of the column, and at the side of a hunted man.

AHIEZER. The son of Ammishaddai, prince of the tribe of Dan in the wilderness.
The name signifies, my brother is help, or brother of help.
He offered on the tenth day at the dedication of the altar, Numbers 7:66-71.
A second Ahiezer, a Benjamite, was chief of the men who came to David at Ziklag.
scriptures: Num 1:12
Of Dan; Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai.
Num 2:25
The standard of the camp of Dan shall be on the north side by their armies: and the captain of the children of Dan shall be Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai.
Num 7:66
On the tenth day Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai, prince of the children of Dan, offered:
The chief was Ahiezer, then Joash, the sons of Shemaah the Gibeathite; and Jeziel, and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; and Berachah, and Jehu the Antothite,
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the rearward is a post of honour, not a place of leftovers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The name is obscure and uncontested; what is easily lost is the weight of the position Ahiezer held.

The principle to recover is God's estimate of the rear guard. Dan was the hindmost of all the camps, and the last place in a marching column is where the weary fall out, where the sick lag, and where an enemy strikes first. Ahiezer's post for forty years was to bring up that end of Israel. Isaiah takes exactly this military picture and applies it to the LORD Himself — the God of Israel will be your rereward — and Moses had said that the eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms. A name meaning my brother is help at the back of the column is a small sermon. The church has always needed men content to march last and count heads, and the second Ahiezer shows the same instinct: he went to David when David was hunted, which is when help is worth something.

pos: n. (a servant of king Josiah sent to Huldah; also Levites and a Simeonite of the same name; Hebrew Asayah)
etymology: Hebrew Asayah, ‘the LORD hath made’ or ‘wrought’ — from asah, to do or make, with the divine name.
biblical_def: Asaiah is named among the five men king Josiah sent when the book of the law was found in the house of the LORD. The king had rent his clothes at the reading, and he commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam, Abdon, Shaphan the scribe, and “Asaiah a servant of the king's” (2Ch 34:20) to enquire of the LORD concerning the words of the book. The delegation went to Huldah the prophetess, and brought back the word that the LORD would indeed bring evil upon the place, but not in Josiah's days, because his heart was tender and he had humbled himself. Asaiah is styled simply the king's servant — the layman in a company of priests and scribes — and he is trusted with the errand on which the reformation turned. The name belongs to others: a Levite of the sons of Merari (1Ch 6:30), the firstborn of the Shilonites who dwelt at Jerusalem after the captivity (1Ch 9:5), and a prince of Simeon among those who drove out the Hamites from their pasture (1Ch 4:36).

Shimea his son, Haggiah his son, Asaiah his son.

corruption_summary: Josiah's response to the recovered book is admired as sincerity of feeling, when the text presents it as submission to a word that condemned him.
corruption_paragraphs: The scene Asaiah was sent into is often reduced to an emotional one: a young king moved by an old book. What actually happens is harder and better. The law is read, and it pronounces against Judah; Josiah does not soften it, does not enquire whether it applies to his times, and does not look for a second opinion. He sends to a prophetess to learn how bad it truly is. The errand assumes the book has authority over the throne that received it. That is the reformation in miniature, and it is why the LORD's answer singles out the king's tender heart — not his feelings, but his yielding.

The principle to recover is the standing of an ordinary servant in such a moment. Asaiah is the one man in the five with no office named — not priest, not scribe, not son of a notable — and he goes with the rest to hear a word that will govern the kingdom. Reformation has never been carried by clergy alone. It moves through households and servants and men whose only description in the record is that they belonged to somebody and were sent. The name says the LORD hath made; the errand shows what He makes such men for.

pos: n. (a priest made treasurer by Nehemiah; and several men of Jeremiah's day; Hebrew Shelemyah)
etymology: Hebrew Shelemyah, ‘the LORD is recompense’ or ‘whom the LORD repays’ — from shalam, to be complete, to make good, to requite.
biblical_def: Shelemiah is a name carried by several men in the last books of the Old Testament, and the most instructive is the priest Nehemiah appointed over the treasuries. Having found the house of God forsaken and the Levites fled to their fields for want of their portions, Nehemiah set treasurers over the stores — “Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and of the Levites, Pedaiah… for they were counted faithful” (Neh 13:13). That is the whole reason given for the appointment, and it is the only qualification named. Others of the name stand in Jeremiah's narrative on both sides. Jehudi, sent to fetch Baruch's roll before the princes, is a son of Shelemiah's line (Jer 36:14); and it was Irijah the son of Shelemiah, a captain of the ward, who seized Jeremiah in the gate of Benjamin and charged him with falling away to the Chaldeans (Jer 37:13). A Shelemiah is also the father of Hananiah who repaired a piece of the wall.

SHELEMIAH. A priest whom Nehemiah made treasurer over the treasuries of the house of God.
The name signifies, Jehovah is recompense, or repayment.
Several men of this name appear in the history of Jeremiah.
It is a compound of shalam, to requite or make good, with the divine name.
scriptures: And I made treasurers over the treasuries, Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and of the Levites, Pedaiah: and next to them was Hanan the son of Zaccur, the son of Mattaniah: for they were counted faithful, and their office was to distribute unto their brethren.
Neh 3:30
After him repaired Hananiah the son of Shelemiah, and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph, another piece. After him repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah over against his chamber.

Therefore all the princes sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, unto Baruch, saying, Take in thine hand the roll wherein thou hast read in the ears of the people, and come. So Baruch the son of Neriah took the roll in his hand, and came unto them.

And when he was in the gate of Benjamin, a captain of the ward was there, whose name was Irijah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Hananiah; and he took Jeremiah the prophet, saying, Thou fallest away to the Chaldeans.
corruption_summary: Faithfulness is treated as the modest virtue left when ability is lacking, though Nehemiah names it as the entire qualification for handling the church's money.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 13:13 gives one reason for the appointment of these treasurers: they were counted faithful. Not that they were skilled accountants, not that they were prominent, not that they were owed a post — they were reckoned trustworthy, and that settled it. The common instinct is to treat faithfulness as the consolation quality, the thing said of a man when nothing more impressive can be said. Scripture inverts this. It is required in stewards that a man be found faithful, and the Lord's own commendation on the last day is not well done, thou brilliant servant.

The principle to recover is what this appointment was for. The Levites had abandoned the house of God because the portions had not been delivered — a failure of administration had emptied the temple of its ministers. Nehemiah's remedy was not a new law but trustworthy men whose office was to distribute unto their brethren. Honest handling of ordinary money is a spiritual office, and its neglect scatters a congregation as surely as false doctrine. The two Shelemiahs of Jeremiah's day are a useful contrast: one line produced a man who fetched the prophet's roll, another produced the captain who arrested the prophet at the gate. The name meant the LORD recompenses. He does, both ways.

pos: n. (father of Esther; also a Levite of Merari and other persons; Hebrew Abichayil)
etymology: Hebrew Abichayil, ‘my father is might’ — from ab, father, and chayil, strength, valour, the same word in the virtuous woman of Proverbs 31.
biblical_def: Abihail is best known as the father of Esther. He is never introduced in his own scene; he is named only in the two places where the writer wishes to fix Esther's descent — when her turn came to go in unto the king she is “the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai” (Est 2:15), and when the second letter of Purim is confirmed she is again “Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail” (Est 9:29). The two mentions bracket the book: one at her lowest exposure, one at her greatest authority. From the first we learn what mattered most about him — he was dead, and his daughter had been taken by Mordecai for his own. The name belongs to others: Zuriel's father among the Merarite Levites who pitched on the north side of the tabernacle (Num 3:35), the wife of Abishur in Judah's line (1Ch 2:29), a Gadite chief, and the mother of Rehoboam's wife. The name means my father is might, and Esther's story is of a fatherless girl whose might was elsewhere.

ABIHAIL. The father of queen Esther and brother of Mordecai's father.
The name signifies, my father is might, or father of strength.
It is borne also by the father of Zuriel, chief of the Merarite Levites.
The same name is given to women, as the wife of Abishur in 1 Chronicles 2:29.
scriptures: Est 2:15

Now when the turn of Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her for his daughter, was come to go in unto the king, she required nothing but what Hegai the king's chamberlain, the keeper of the women, appointed. And Esther obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her.
Est 9:29
Then Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew, wrote with all authority, to confirm this second letter of Purim.
Num 3:35
And the chief of the house of the father of the families of Merari was Zuriel the son of Abihail: these shall pitch on the side of the tabernacle northward.
And the name of the wife of Abishur was Abihail, and she bare him Ahban, and Molid.
corruption_summary: Esther is read as a self-made heroine who seized her moment, when the book is careful to show a fatherless captive girl placed where she did not choose to be.
corruption_paragraphs: Esther is regularly retold as a story of ambition rewarded — a girl who made the most of her opportunity. Her father's name is one of the details that resists this. She is the daughter of Abihail, which is to say she is an orphan; Mordecai took her for his own daughter because she had neither father nor mother. She did not enter the palace by choice but by a royal levy on the young women of the provinces. And in the verse that names her father, she is commended for asking for nothing — she required nothing but what Hegai appointed. That is the opposite of a woman working an angle.

The principle to recover is providence, which is the doctrine the book of Esther exists to teach and which it teaches without once naming God. Every hinge of the story is a coincidence too well-timed to be one: a king's insomnia, a chronicle read aloud at the right page, a gallows built for the wrong man. Into that pattern the orphan is set, and Mordecai puts the question that names it — who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this. Her father's name says my father is might. Abihail was in his grave, and the might held.

etymology: Hebrew Basemath, from bosem, spice, balsam, sweet savour — a name meaning fragrance, given to a woman whose marriage was a grief of mind to Isaac and Rebekah.
biblical_def: Bashemath is named among the wives of Esau. Genesis 26:34 records that at forty years old Esau took Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite — and the next verse adds that they were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah. A second Bashemath is named in the genealogy of Genesis 36 as Ishmael's daughter, sister of Nebajoth, who bare Reuel to Esau (Gen 36:3-4); the lists of Esau's wives in chapters 26, 28 and 36 use overlapping names, a feature of the record that has occupied readers since antiquity. What is not in doubt is the pattern. Esau married into Canaan and into Ishmael, outside the line and outside the promise, while Jacob was sent to Padanaram expressly so that he should not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan. The whole difference between the two brothers, already declared at the selling of the birthright, is visible again in whom each of them married.

webster_full: The proper name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary.
BASHEMATH. A wife of Esau, daughter of Elon the Hittite.
The name signifies fragrance, or sweet spice, from bosem, balsam.
A Bashemath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebajoth, is also named as Esau's wife.
The form Basmath is used of a daughter of Solomon in 1 Kings 4:15.
scriptures: And Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite:
Gen 36:3
And Bashemath Ishmael's daughter, sister of Nebajoth.
Gen 36:4
And Adah bare to Esau Eliphaz; and Bashemath bare Reuel;
And these are the sons of Reuel; Nahath, and Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah: these were the sons of Bashemath Esau's wife.
corruption_summary: The command that Jacob not marry the daughters of Canaan is read as ethnic preference, when Scripture consistently makes the issue covenant and worship rather than blood.
corruption_paragraphs: Esau's Hittite marriages are sometimes cited as evidence that the patriarchs practised a bare racial exclusivity. The text will not support it. Rahab the Canaanite of Jericho and Ruth the Moabitess both marry into Israel and both stand in the genealogy of Christ, honoured without qualification; the bar that fell on the daughters of Canaan was never their descent but their gods, and the reason given for it in Deuteronomy is explicit — they will turn away thy son from following me. Where a woman of the nations turned to the LORD, as Ruth did in as clear a confession as the Old Testament contains, she was received into the covenant people and into the royal line.

The principle to recover is that marriage is a covenantal act before it is a personal one, and Esau's is the standing example of a man who did not think so. He is called a profane person in Hebrews, and the word means one who treats holy things as common. He sold a birthright for a meal and he married where he pleased, and both were the same sin appearing twice. The apostolic rule keeps the principle and drops nothing: a widow is at liberty to be married to whom she will, only in the Lord. Bashemath's name meant fragrance, and Genesis records the marriage as a bitterness of spirit to the man and woman who had raised him.

pos: n. (a descendant of Saul through Jonathan, in the Benjamite genealogies; Hebrew Atsel)
etymology: Hebrew Atsel, from a root meaning to set aside, reserve, or lay up beside — a fitting name for a man whose whole significance is that a line was kept.
biblical_def: Azel is a man of Benjamin, descended from Saul through Jonathan by way of Mephibosheth, Micah, and their sons. He appears in the Chronicler's Benjamite genealogy and again, almost word for word, in the register of those who dwelt at Jerusalem after the captivity: “And Azel had six sons, whose names are these, Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan” (1Ch 8:38). Nothing is told of him but his father, his six sons, and the fact that the same list was worth writing twice. That is the point of him. Saul's house had been struck down at Gilboa, hunted through the years of David's rise, and reduced at last to a lame child hidden at Lodebar. The dynasty was finished. Yet centuries later, when the exiles came home and the Chronicler set out to show that Israel still existed, the line of the rejected king was still there to be counted, six sons deep, living in Jerusalem. Azel is the evidence that God's rejection of a throne was not the extinction of a family.

AZEL. A Benjamite, descended from king Saul through Jonathan and Mephibosheth.
The Hebrew root signifies to set aside, to reserve, or to lay up beside.
His six sons are named identically in 1 Chronicles 8:38 and 1 Chronicles 9:44.
A place named Azal is mentioned in Zechariah 14:5, from a kindred form.
scriptures: And Moza begat Binea: Rapha was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son:
And Azel had six sons, whose names are these, Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel.
And Moza begat Binea; and Rephaiah his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son.
And Azel had six sons, whose names are these, Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan: these were the sons of Azel.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's judgment on an office is not the annihilation of a household.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Azel is a name in a list twice repeated, and no one contests him. The temptation is simply to skip both lists.

The principle to recover is the difference between a judgment and an erasure. The LORD rejected Saul from being king, and the sentence was executed — the kingdom was rent from him and given to a neighbour better than he, and his sons fell with him in one day on Gilboa. But the sentence fell on the throne, not on the blood. David sought out whether any remained of the house of Saul that he might shew him kindness for Jonathan's sake, and set Mephibosheth at his own table continually. From that preserved cripple the line ran down through Micah and Moza to Azel and his six sons, and was still in Jerusalem after the exile, still worth a full entry. God is exact in His judgments and never wasteful with them. He removed a crown and kept a family, and He noted their names twice so that no one reading would think the house had simply vanished.
roots_summary: Hebrew Atsel (H682), Azel; from atsal (H680), to set aside, reserve, lay up beside.
roots_lines: Hebrew Atsel (H682) — Azel, a Benjamite of Saul's house; 1 Chronicles 8:37-38, 9:43-44.
Hebrew atsal (H680) — to lay aside, reserve, keep back; Numbers 11:17.
Hebrew Merib-baal / Mephibosheth (H4648) — Jonathan's son, in this line; 2 Samuel 9:6.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — kindness; the ground of David's dealing with the house, 2 Samuel 9:1.
The genealogy is given twice, in the Benjamite list and among the dwellers at Jerusalem.
usage: “Azel had six sons” — the same six names recorded twice over.
“All these were the sons of Azel” — a rejected house still counted.
“Eleasah his son, Azel his son” — Saul's line traced past the exile.

pos: n. (a Levite who helped the people understand the law; and several others; Hebrew Chanan)
etymology: Hebrew Chanan, ‘gracious’ or ‘he hath shewn favour’ — from chanan, to bend or stoop in kindness to an inferior, the root behind grace, Hannah, John, and Hananiah.
biblical_def: Hanan is a common name in the returned community, and its most notable bearer stands in one of the great scenes of the Old Testament. When Ezra read the book of the law before the congregation at the water gate, a company of Levites moved among the people, and Hanan is named among them: they “caused the people to understand the law: and the people stood in their place” (Neh 8:7). They gave the sense and caused them to understand the reading — the first plain description in Scripture of exposition as an office. A Hanan is among those who sealed the covenant (Neh 10:10), and another, son of Zaccur, was set next to Nehemiah's treasurers because they were counted faithful (Neh 13:13). One more appears in Jeremiah: the sons of Hanan the son of Igdaliah, a man of God, had a chamber in the house of the LORD, and it was there that Jeremiah set wine before the Rechabites to test their obedience (Jer 35:4).

HANAN. A Levite who assisted Ezra in expounding the law to the people.
The name signifies gracious, or he hath shewn favour.
It is from the same root as Hannah, Hananiah, and the Greek form John.
Several men of the name appear in Nehemiah and one in Jeremiah 35.

Also Jeshua, and Bani, and Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodijah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites, caused the people to understand the law: and the people stood in their place.
And their brethren, Shebaniah, Hodijah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan,

And I made treasurers over the treasuries, Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and of the Levites, Pedaiah: and next to them was Hanan the son of Zaccur, the son of Mattaniah: for they were counted faithful, and their office was to distribute unto their brethren.
Jer 35:4

And I brought them into the house of the LORD, into the chamber of the sons of Hanan, the son of Igdaliah, a man of God, which was by the chamber of the princes, which was above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, the keeper of the door:
corruption_summary: Preaching is widely reduced to inspiration or commentary on the times, when Nehemiah 8 defines it as causing a congregation to understand a text.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 8 is the oldest job description a preacher has, and it is narrow. They read in the book distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading. Three things, all of them tied to a text that already existed: read it so it can be heard, give what it means, and keep at it until the people have it. Nothing is said about originality, and the men doing it are not the celebrated figures of the chapter — Ezra reads, and a dozen Levites including Hanan work through the congregation making sure it lands. Where preaching becomes a platform for the speaker's own material, or a survey of the week's events with a verse attached, this office has been abandoned whatever else is happening.

The principle to recover is the aim of the exposition. The people stood in their place while it was read, and they wept when they understood the words; then they were sent away to eat the fat and drink the sweet, because the joy of the LORD was their strength. Understanding came first and did its proper work — conviction, then joy, then generosity to them for whom nothing was prepared. The name Hanan means gracious. A man who spends his life making a hard text plain to ordinary people is doing a work well described by it.

The same root yields Hannah, Hananiah, Johanan, and the Greek form John.

“The people stood in their place” — a congregation on its feet under the word.
“The sons of Hanan… a man of God” — a chamber in the house of the LORD.

pos: n. (several men, including the owner of the dungeon into which Jeremiah was cast; Hebrew Malkiyah)
etymology: Hebrew Malkiyah, ‘the LORD is my king’ — from melek, king, with the divine name. The KJV also spells it Malchijah.
biblical_def: Malchiah is borne by several men, and two of them stand at opposite ends of the same book. One is Pashur the son of Malchiah, among the princes who heard Jeremiah's preaching and demanded his death, saying that he weakened the hands of the men of war (Jer 38:1). The other gives his name to the pit: “Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison… and in the dungeon there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire” (Jer 38:6). A Malchiah of a very different sort appears in Nehemiah: the son of Rechab, ruler of part of Bethhaccerem, who repaired the dung gate and set up its doors, locks and bars (Neh 3:14). The dung gate was the refuse gate of Jerusalem, the least honourable assignment on the wall, and a ruler took it. The name is also in the priestly genealogy of the sons of Levi (1Ch 6:40). All of them are called by a name that confesses the LORD as king; not all of them lived as though He were.

MALCHIAH. The name of several men in the Old Testament; also written Malchijah.
The name signifies, Jehovah is my king, from melek, a king.
One Malchiah owned the miry dungeon into which Jeremiah was let down with cords.
Another, the son of Rechab, repaired the dung gate of Jerusalem under Nehemiah.
scriptures: Jer 38:1

Then Shephatiah the son of Mattan, and Gedaliah the son of Pashur, and Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashur the son of Malchiah, heard the words that Jeremiah had spoken unto all the people, saying,
Jer 38:6

Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. And in the dungeon there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire.
Neh 3:14
But the dung gate repaired Malchiah the son of Rechab, the ruler of part of Bethhaccerem; he built it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof.
The son of Michael, the son of Baaseiah, the son of Malchiah,
corruption_summary: Faithful speech is judged by whether it strengthens morale, the exact charge laid against Jeremiah before he was put in Malchiah's pit.
corruption_paragraphs: The princes did not accuse Jeremiah of lying. Their charge was that he weakened the hands of the men of war and sought not the welfare of the people but the hurt — that is, his message was bad for morale, and therefore he had to be silenced. It is a permanently available argument, and its power is that it never has to engage the question of whether the thing said is true. A prophet who is right at the wrong moment is still, on this reasoning, a traitor. Zedekiah, who believed Jeremiah and feared his own princes, gave him up with the most cowardly sentence in the book: he is in your hand, for the king is not he that can do any thing against you.

The principle to recover is that truth is not measured by its effect on confidence. Jeremiah was let down into the mire for saying what God had told him to say, and the word he spoke came true within two years. Set against him is the other Malchiah on the wall in Nehemiah, a ruler who took the dung gate — the refuse gate, the humblest station on the whole circuit — and built it with its doors and locks and bars. Both men are named for the same confession, that the LORD is king. One line of the family owned the pit; another repaired the gate nobody wanted. The name settles nothing; the life shows what it was worth.
